🚨 ELECTION INTEGRITY TIMELINE — ANOTHER PIECE JUST DROPPED

President Trump formally extended Executive Order 13848, keeping America’s national emergency concerning foreign interference in U.S. elections in effect for another year — through September 12, 2027.

EO 13848 was originally signed by Trump on September 12, 2018.

The underlying declaration treats attempted foreign interference in American elections as an **“unusual and extraordinary threat” to the national security and foreign policy of the United States.

The renewed emergency addresses threats including:

🔹 Unauthorized access to election and campaign infrastructure
🔹 Cyber operations targeting the electoral process
🔹 Covert propaganda and disinformation
🔹 Foreign efforts designed to interfere with elections or undermine public confidence

And the TIMING is what makes this particularly relevant to the timeline we’ve been documenting.

📍 JULY 16 — Trump publicly lays out allegations involving foreign access to U.S. voter-registration information and vulnerabilities surrounding American elections.

📍 JULY 17 — DHS moves into the response as Secretary Markwayne Mullin publicly discusses federal action addressing election-system vulnerabilities.

📍 JULY 24 — Tina Peters and her team present their election-security proposal to CISA.

📍 JULY 30 — The White House formalizes its election-interference intelligence case, alleging foreign acquisition of American voter data and election-infrastructure targeting.

📍 AUGUST 17–18 — DOJ announces plans for approximately 1,000 federal election monitors for the November midterms.

📍 AUGUST 24 — The Supreme Court allows key provisions of Trump’s election executive order to move forward while litigation continues.

📍 AUGUST 24 — DHS reports Chinese-manufactured components in electronic voting machines used in the United States.

📍 AUGUST 26 — Tina Peters releases her proposed “2026 Election Infrastructure Immediate Federal Risk Mitigation Roadmap.”

📍 AUGUST 27 — Reporting emerges regarding movement toward manual audits of paper ballots.

📍 AUGUST 24–28 — The administration advances its USPS/mail-ballot framework involving citizenship-list matching, standardized procedures and ballot identifiers/barcodes.

📍 AUGUST 31 — Trump formally extends the existing ELECTION-INTERFERENCE NATIONAL EMERGENCY through September 2027.

📍 SEPTEMBER 1 — DHS Homeland Security Investigations launches a coordinated criminal voter-fraud investigation surge.

And now there’s an important nuance to understand about the August 31 action.

⚠️ FOREIGN INTERFERENCE DOESN’T NECESSARILY MEAN EVERYTHING HAPPENS OVERSEAS.

The presidential notice specifically continues the national emergency concerning FOREIGN interference in U.S. elections.

But that does not necessarily mean the conduct being investigated would have to occur entirely outside the United States.

If U.S.-based individuals, organizations, companies or other domestic actors were working with, acting on behalf of, materially assisting, or serving as intermediaries for covered foreign actors, their domestic activity could potentially fall within authorities triggered by foreign interference — depending upon the conduct involved and the particular legal authority being exercised.

If investigators ultimately established a qualifying foreign-domestic connection, the fact that some alleged conduct occurred inside the United States would not necessarily place it outside the broader legal framework.

And THAT is why the timing deserves attention.

Trump didn’t create a new election-related national emergency on August 31.

He affirmatively continued the one established in 2018, ensuring that the emergency remains active throughout the entire 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION and well into 2027.

Another date goes on the board:

➡️ 8/31/26 — TRUMP EXTENDS EO 13848 / ELECTION-INTERFERENCE NATIONAL EMERGENCY

The timeline continues to grow.

🔔 Kalshi ruling puts CFTC prediction rules at risk 

⚠️ A federal appeals court ruled on Aug. 28 that Kalshi had not shown Nevada’s regulation of its sports-event contracts was likely preempted by federal commodities law. The unanimous decision allows Nevada gaming authorities to enforce state requirements while litigation continues.

⚠️ Kalshi argued that its sports-event contracts qualified as swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act. Because Kalshi operates a CFTC-regulated designated contract market, it said federal jurisdiction displaced Nevada’s gaming laws. The Ninth Circuit rejected that argument at the preliminary-injunction stage. It found that the contracts likely fell outside the applicable meaning of “swap” because they functioned as sports bets. The panel consequently rejected Kalshi’s express, conflict and field-preemption arguments.

📣 Circuit Judge Ryan Nelson wrote that “the CFTC is not a national gambling regulator.” The court said Kalshi’s broader interpretation lacked a limiting principle and did not fit the surrounding statutory framework. That prediction extends beyond the court’s direct holding. The opinion said Kalshi’s broad interpretation of “swap” “would raise concerns under the major-questions doctrine.” It did not hold that the doctrine categorically prevents the CFTC from regulating prediction markets.

Essentially, funds have found a way to turn a very ordinary local business into companies worth billions of dollars.
